query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs, regions with higher initial Mg supersaturation (e.g., via a compositional gradient) undergo selective, diffusion-driven oxidation during high-temperature and corrosive exposures. This process leads to the formation of a continuous or semi-continuous Mg-rich oxide/intermetallic interface that alters passivation behavior, thereby modifying the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation performance relative to a baseline homogeneous structure.
generation.material_initial_state: Non-equilibrium-processed lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ that consist of a mixture of metastable solid solution regions and stable intermetallic compounds, with controlled variations in initial Mg distribution (homogeneous vs. compositional gradient).
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the initial Mg distribution by producing one set of HEA samples with a homogeneous Mg distribution and another set with a compositional gradient resulting in regions of enhanced Mg supersaturation.
generation.conditions: Expose both sets of samples to accelerated aging conditions, including high-temperature oxidation (e.g., around 700°C in an oxidative atmosphere) and corrosive environments (e.g., salt spray or NaCl solution), while maintaining the density constraint and non-equilibrium microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous or semi-continuous Mg-rich oxide layer and associated intermetallic phases at the microstructural interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Upon exposure to high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments, Mg diffuses from metastable solid solution regions and preferentially oxidizes at phase boundaries. This diffusion-driven oxidation promotes the nucleation and growth of stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds and continuous oxide layers that alter the passivation behavior and structural stability of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: The samples with compositional gradients (higher local Mg supersaturation) will exhibit a more pronounced evolution into Mg-rich oxide and intermetallic phases compared to the homogeneous samples. This difference will manifest as either enhanced corrosion resistance (through effective passivation) or accelerated degradation if the oxide layer becomes disrupted, relative to the baseline homogeneous microstructure.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous non-equilibrium Mg-containing HEA samples with a uniform Mg distribution.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds under conditions where the alloy density remains below 6 g/cm³ and the initial processing leads to a mix of metastable and stable phases, and when exposed to controlled high-temperature oxidation and corrosive environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative differences in Mg diffusion kinetics, the critical threshold of Mg supersaturation necessary for forming a continuous oxide layer, and whether the resulting interface always enhances or sometimes accelerates degradation remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Mg-containing lightweight HEA samples: one with a homogeneous Mg distribution and one with a controlled compositional gradient leading to localized Mg supersaturation. Subject both sets to identical accelerated aging conditions including high-temperature oxidation (e.g., 700°C in air) and exposure to a corrosive medium (e.g., salt spray or NaCl solution).
measurements: Characterization of microstructural evolution using SEM/TEM and EDS to detect and map Mg-rich oxide/intermetallic formation at interfaces.
Electrochemical corrosion rate measurements to quantify differences in passivation behavior.
Mass gain measurements during oxidation tests to assess the progression of oxidation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiment shows no significant difference in the formation of Mg-rich oxide/interface layers or if the corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behaviors are statistically similar between the homogeneous and gradient samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

frame.system: Non-equilibrium, Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ that exhibit a mix of solid solution regions and stable intermetallic compounds, initially produced by processes such as induction melting and compositional grading.
frame.goal: To explain the mechanistic evolution of the alloy’s microstructure (from metastable states toward equilibrium phases) and correlate this transformation process with changes in its corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
frame.limitation: Prior work has focused largely on hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving the evolution pathways—particularly those affecting high-temperature oxidation and corrosion—underexplored. The structural complexity due in part to constituent-property differences promotes stable intermetallic phases, obscuring the transformation mechanisms from metastable to equilibrium states.
root_cause_cues: constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds
constraints: presence of both solid solution and intermetallic phases
non-equilibrium processing conditions (e.g., induction melting, compositional grading)
frame.regime: The hypothesis applies under conditions where the alloy is subjected to accelerated aging, corrosion, and high-temperature oxidation environments that promote phase evolution from metastable to stable states. Testing under controlled temperature, oxidative atmospheres, and corrosive media is implied.
prior_attempts: Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys that captured structural complexity without resolving transformation mechanisms.
Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys that demonstrated region-dependent mechanical and corrosion performance.
Studies on AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys which correlated Mg content with phase stability and multiple properties, yet focused predominantly on hardness and room-temperature compression.
frame.understanding: The hypothesis posits that during exposure to aggressive oxidation and corrosion environments, the non-equilibrium Mg-containing high-entropy alloys undergo a selective, diffusion-driven phase transformation where magnesium is preferentially oxidized and segregates to specific microstructural interfaces. This alters the local chemistry and microstructure by either dissolving metastable phases or promoting the nucleation of stable intermetallic compounds. The formation of a continuous or semi-continuous Mg-rich oxide layer at interfaces acts as a passivating barrier that either enhances corrosion resistance and oxidation behavior or, if disrupted, results in accelerated degradation. A controlled comparison might involve alloy samples aged under identical thermal and chemical conditions with and without a pre-established microstructural gradient, predicting that regions with initially higher metastability (more solute Mg in a supersaturated solid solution) will display a more pronounced evolution (e.g., formation of distinct Mg-rich intermetallics or oxides) and concomitantly different corrosion/oxidation rates relative to the baseline homogeneous microstructure. Boundary conditions include maintaining the density constraint, ensuring non-equilibrium starting structures, and exposing the samples to designated high-temperature oxidation and corrosion environments. Prior observations of microstructural heterogeneity and region-dependent behavior support the idea of diffusional instabilities and selective phase evolution. An outcome falsifying the hypothesis would be if controlled testing reveals no significant difference in the evolution of microstructure or in corrosion/high-temperature oxidation behavior between samples that differ in initial metastability or Mg distribution.

decision.trend: Early work on lightweight complex concentrated and high-entropy alloys demonstrated that non‐equilibrium processing (for example, induction melting, spark plasma sintering, and compositional grading) produces microstructures that mix metastable solid solution regions with stable intermetallic compounds. Subsequent studies then correlated Mg (or Mg‐containing systems) with phase stability and region‐dependent mechanical and corrosion properties. However, while these studies revealed that Mg distribution appears to influence both local phase evolution and performance under corrosive and high-temperature oxidation conditions, they have not yet pinpointed a clear diffusion‐driven transformation mechanism from metastable to equilibrium states.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue is how preferential oxidation and segregation of magnesium at microstructural interfaces during accelerated aging controls the transition from metastable solid solutions to stable intermetallic/oxide phases, and consequently alters the corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior. In particular, it remains untested whether the formation (or breakdown) of a continuous Mg‐rich oxide interface relates directly to improved passivation or accelerated degradation.
decision.lever: Systematically vary the initial Mg distribution (e.g., contrasting homogeneous versus compositional gradient microstructures) in non-equilibrium processed lightweight HEA samples and expose them to controlled high-temperature and corrosive environments
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend of region-dependent transformation observed in prior work. By controlling the initial spatial distribution of Mg, one can directly test whether regions with higher Mg supersaturation undergo a preferential diffusion‐mediated transformation—forming continuous Mg-rich oxides or intermetallic phases—that correlates with altered corrosion and oxidation behavior. Such a controlled comparison will provide a clear mechanistic test on the role of Mg in the evolution pathway.
